title: Has India really ended poverty? What the World Bank's 2026 report shows, and why economists still argue
standfirst: About 2 in 100 Indians live below the World Bank's extreme poverty line, roughly Rs 68 a day. About 79 in 100 live below its line for upper-middle-income countries, the group India hopes to join, roughly Rs 187 a day. Both are true. Here is how, and why the argument over India's poverty numbers will not go away.

short.headline: India has nearly escaped extreme poverty. Most Indians have not escaped poverty
short.dek: About 2 in 100 Indians were below $3 a day in 2024, roughly Rs 68. About 15 in 100 were below India's peer line of $4.20, and 79 in 100 below the $8.30 line of richer countries.
short.body: Both numbers come from the same household spending data. The World Bank's extreme line sits at about the level of India's last official poverty line carried forward for prices, and its measure counts the free ration grain that more than 80 crore people receive. Most Indians live just above it: a 10% fall in spending would push the share below Rs 95 a day from 15% to 23%. Between 2014-15 and 2024-25, real GDP per person grew about 62%, while a farm labourer's real wage grew about 9%. How far poverty has fallen is genuinely disputed, because the survey changed in 2022-23 and India has no official poverty line.

macha: Okay, here's the deal. Almost nobody in India is below the World Bank's rock-bottom line any more, about Rs 68 a day, and free ration grain is part of why. But about 15 in 100 Indians are below the line for countries like India, Rs 95 a day, and 79 in 100 are below the richer-country line of Rs 187. Most people live in between, close enough that a 10% fall in everyone's spending would push the share below Rs 95 from 15% to 23%. In ten years GDP per person has grown about 62% and a farm labourer's real wage about 9%, and nobody knows exactly how far poverty fell because the survey changed. So when someone says India has ended poverty, ask: at which line?
audience: A curious Indian adult who has heard that India has ended extreme poverty and wants to know whether it is true and what it means.
heroDescription: Three lines, one for each World Bank poverty line: the lowest has almost emptied, the highest has not.

pullQuotes.quote: When the World Bank calls its line extreme, it is drawing it at about the level India itself once called the poverty line.

boxes.term: poverty line (where do $3, $4.20 and $8.30 come from?)
boxes.plainMeaning: The World Bank sets its global lines from the poverty lines countries set for themselves. $3 a day is the typical line of the world's poorest countries. $4.20 is typical of lower-middle-income countries, India's own group. $8.30 is typical of upper-middle-income countries such as those India hopes to join. All three are in 2021 prices and converted with purchasing power parity, not the exchange rate.
boxes.whyItMattersHere: None of the lines measures a decent life. They measure how India compares with the standards other countries set. The $4.20 line is the fairest test of India against its peers.

boxes.term: purchasing power parity (why use dollars for India?)
boxes.plainMeaning: A dollar buys more in Patna than in Pittsburgh, because many goods and especially services cost less in India. Purchasing power parity, or PPP, compares what money actually buys across countries, using prices collected for the same basket of goods everywhere. For India, one PPP dollar was worth about Rs 19.47 in 2021 prices. The World Bank then adjusts each household's spending for price differences between states and between villages and cities before applying that single national factor.
boxes.whyItMattersHere: PPP makes India comparable with other countries, but it is an average basket, not yours. When the price data were updated in 2025, India's extreme poverty rate on the same survey rose from 1.0% to 2.6%, with no change in anyone's life.

boxes.term: Rangarajan (Tendulkar or Rangarajan: where should India's line be?)
boxes.plainMeaning: The Tendulkar line of 2011-12 was Rs 816 a person a month in villages and Rs 1,000 in towns, and found 21.9% of Indians poor. The Rangarajan group in 2014 rebuilt the line from what people need to eat (calories, protein and fat) plus essential non-food spending. Its line was Rs 972 and Rs 1,407, and found 29.5% poor. Those who favoured the higher line argued the old one described destitution. Those against it argued a higher line would sweep in households that were not poor by any ordinary meaning.
boxes.whyItMattersHere: Neither line was ever replaced, so the choice of line is still the biggest single reason Indian poverty estimates differ. Our read: the Tendulkar line, carried forward for prices, is close to the World Bank's $3 line, and both are lines for destitution, not for poverty as most Indians would understand it.

boxes.term: consumption survey (did the 2022-23 redesign shrink poverty?)
boxes.plainMeaning: India measures poverty from what households spend, collected by the National Statistics Office. The 2022-23 survey changed the method: three visits instead of one, three separate questionnaires and longer lists of items. The World Bank also switched its earlier figures to the same recall method, which lowered its 2011-12 rate. Supporters of the new design say it records spending more fully. Critics say the change makes the fall since 2011-12 look larger than it was, and that the withheld 2017-18 survey showed spending falling.
boxes.whyItMattersHere: Bridging estimates that try to correct for the change put 2022-23 poverty well above the World Bank's direct reading, though still far below 2011-12. Our read: the fall is real, its size is uncertain, and only a survey whose design stays fixed can settle it.

boxes.term: Gini index (is India really the fourth most equal country?)
boxes.plainMeaning: The Gini index measures inequality on a scale from 0, where everyone has the same, to 100, where one person has everything. India's figure of 25.5, quoted by the government, comes from what households spend. Most countries report the Gini of income, which is always higher, because richer people save much of what they earn. Ranking a spending Gini against income Ginis compares different things.
boxes.whyItMattersHere: India's spending Gini did fall between the two new surveys, and the poorest gained most. Even converted to an income basis, the World Bank does not class India as highly unequal. But the survey misses much of the top, and income and wealth data show the richest 1% with a larger share than at any time since 1922. Our read: not among the most unequal, and far from the fourth most equal.

caveats: The World Bank's figures after 2023-24 are estimates carried forward from the last survey using growth forecasts, not new measurements.
The 2022-23 and 2023-24 surveys were redesigned and are not directly comparable with 2011-12; part of the measured fall may come from the change in method.
India has no survey reading in the World Bank's database between 2011-12 and 2022-23.
The World Bank's spending measure includes free and subsidised ration grain at local market value. It does not include free health care or education.
Rupee equivalents of the dollar lines are national averages at 2023-24 prices, not separate rural and urban budgets.

The wage index covers men's daily wage rates in three rural occupations and factory workers' pay per day worked. It does not measure household income, women's wages or the number of days people find work.
Child stunting (2019-21), health-spending hardship (2022) and the World Bank's multidimensional measure (2022-23) cover different populations and years and cannot be added.
Statements by NITI Aayog, SBI Research, the Press Information Bureau and individual researchers are reported as their published claims.
